records.title: roadmap: graph traversal as local reasoning layer
records.body:
## Background

CBrain will be used over a long time horizon, so the knowledge graph will keep growing in both entity count and relation density. LLM and embedding latency can be mitigated with caching, batching, async jobs, and graceful degradation, but the local graph layer is deterministic infrastructure that can keep improving as the brain grows.

This issue records the long-term direction: treat graph traversal and graph algorithms as a first-class local reasoning layer, not just as a helper for `graph_query`.

## Product Goal

Make CBrain better at answering relation-heavy and context-heavy questions without relying on extra LLM calls when deterministic graph evidence is enough.

The graph layer should improve:

- multi-hop recall speed
- explainable relationship paths
- hierarchy and organization traversal
- local relevance ranking
- discovery of meaningful clusters and bridge nodes
- lower latency for graph-heavy recall paths

## Capability Direction

Future phases may include:

- unified traversal core for graph-facing tools and recall internals
- batched BFS / DFS traversal with relation, trust, weight, and depth constraints
- in-memory graph snapshot or adjacency index backed by SQLite as source of truth
- shortest path and weighted path search
- personalized PageRank or local centrality scoring around a query/session/topic
- community detection for long-term clusters
- bridge / isolation signals for discovery
- temporal graph traversal and graph diff summaries
- native implementation only if benchmarks show TypeScript/SQLite or JS in-memory traversal is insufficient

## Design Guardrails

- SQLite remains the authoritative persistent store.
- Graph algorithms must preserve provenance, trust_state, confidence, relation type, and source_type semantics.
- The local graph layer must not fabricate relationships or upgrade candidate evidence into trusted facts.
- Simple recall must remain fast and predictable; graph-heavy paths should be invoked only when they add clear value.
- Any cache or snapshot must have clear invalidation after link mutation, page merge, deletion, or trust-state update.
- Public examples, tests, and docs must use anonymized placeholders only.

## Non-goals

- Do not rewrite CBrain in C/Rust/Zig.
- Do not introduce a full Cypher engine as the first step.
- Do not move ontology, NER, provenance, or write governance into a native module.
- Do not add opaque graph ranking that cannot be explained from stored edges.

## First Implementation Slice

Start with a small implementation issue that unifies graph traversal hot paths and adds benchmarks before considering lower-level native work.

records.title: Fase 7: Comment, list comment, delete comment, reply
records.body:
## Context
US-07, US-10 (P1), FR-FEED-03/04. Comment count termasuk reply; delete parent menghapus semua reply via `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

## Scope
- `api-gateway/handlers/social.go`
- `api-gateway/routes.go`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `POST /api/videos/:id/comments` validasi `content` 1–1000 karakter; video accessible dan `READY`; transaction `InsertComment` + `IncrementCommentsCount`; return `201`.
- [ ] Insert notifikasi `type=comment` ke owner jika bukan owner.
- [ ] `GET /api/videos/:id/comments` return flat list `created_at DESC` dengan cursor pagination.
- [ ] `DELETE /api/comments/:id` owner only; transaction `CountCommentSubtree` + `DeleteCommentByID` + `DecrementCommentsCount(subtree)`; return `204`.
- [ ] `POST /api/comments/:id/reply` parent harus ada, video accessible dan `READY`; `InsertComment` dengan `parent_id`; return `201`; kirim notifikasi ke video owner dan parent author.

## Technical Notes
- Composite FK `(parent_id, video_id)` menjamin reply selalu di video yang sama.
- `CountCommentSubtree` memakai recursive CTE.
- `comments_count` di tabel `videos` diupdate dengan jumlah subtree.

records.title: [gdrive-avoma] getFolderStructure does unbounded sequential recursion (N+1 Drive calls)
records.body:
**Severity:** medium · **Dimension:** performance · **Area:** `gdrive-avoma` · **Confidence:** high · **Verdict:** confirmed

**File:** `src/lib/google-drive.ts` (333-356)

### Problem
getFolderStructure lists subfolders then awaits getFolderStructure for each subfolder one-at-a-time inside a for-loop (351-356), recursing to maxDepth=3 by default. For a wide tree this is an N+1 explosion of serial Drive round-trips, with no timeout and no pagination on the subfolder list (no pageToken). getFolderContents similarly issues an extra serial files.get for the parent name (598-602).

### Impact
Folder traversal becomes slow and prone to hitting Drive rate limits; combined with missing timeouts it can hang the request. Latency scales with total node count.

### Recommendation
Parallelize subfolder recursion with bounded-concurrency Promise.all, follow pageToken for subfolder listings, add depth/total-node caps and timeouts, cache parent-name lookups.

---
_Verifier note: Confirmed: serial for-loop recursion at 351-356, no pageToken, default maxDepth 3._

_From automated audit (run `wf_1e6ec62e-08a`). Part of #39._

records.title: A recursive query with computed integer terms fails with a syntax error
records.body:
### Version

1.18.0

### What happened?

I'm using Postgres's RECURSIVE subquery in order to compute an order walk of a tree-like data structure. I've been able to run the query successfully directly with Postgres, but sqlc fails to generate code for it, complaining of a syntax error.

### Relevant log output

```shell
sqlc generate
# package db
query.sql:110:1: edited query syntax is invalid: syntax error at or near "FROM"
```


### Database schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE graphs (
    graph_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    author TEXT,
    script TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE nodes (
    node_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    kind Kind NOT NULL,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    graph UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES graphs(graph_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE edges (
    parent UUID REFERENCES nodes (node_id),
    child UUID REFERENCES nodes (node_id),
    ordinal INT NOT NULL,
    graph UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES graphs(graph_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY(parent, child)
);
```


### SQL queries

```sql
-- name: GetDependentNodes :many
WITH RECURSIVE ds(id, depth) AS (
	SELECT parent AS id, 0
	FROM edges WHERE edges.child=$1
  UNION ALL
	SELECT edges.parent, depth+1
	FROM ds, edges WHERE edges.child=ds.id
)
SELECT * FROM ds ORDER BY depth;
```


### Configuration

```yaml
version: "2"
sql:
  - engine: "postgresql"
    queries: "query.sql"
    schema: "schema.sql"
    gen:
      go:
        package: "db"
        out: "pkg/db"
        sql_package: "pgx/v5"
        emit_json_tags: true
        emit_result_struct_pointers: true
```


### Playground URL

https://play.sqlc.dev/p/5dacbfafc94b7fb76f29f429b91a76819583e5b4691afcb6c48041773822fa3b

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What database engines are you using?

PostgreSQL

### What type of code are you generating?

Go

records.title: refactor(purgeprovenance): route row resets through a transactional repository seam
records.body:
## Summary

`purgeprovenance.resetRows` issues raw `UPDATE`s against `work_queue` and `scan_results` from a
`*sql.DB` it holds directly, duplicating storage contracts that belong to `internal/queue` and
`internal/scan`. Raised by CodeRabbit on #661 and deferred there deliberately: the fix spans two
packages and would have pushed that PR past the size gate.

## What is duplicated

`internal/purgeprovenance/purgeprovenance.go:327-379` restates, in SQL literals, the re-queue
semantics that `queue`/`scan` own:

- the `status` literal the row is reset to
- `priority = -100` (dequeue-eligible but strictly behind foreground work)
- the `next_attempt_at` timestamp format
- clearing `last_error`

The doc comment is explicit that this MIRRORS `ResetInstrumental`'s reset shape. That is the
defect in one sentence: two packages now encode the same reset, and nothing makes them move
together. If `queue` changes its status vocabulary, its priority convention, or its timestamp
format, this file keeps compiling and silently writes rows the queue no longer understands.

Against the repo guideline for `internal/{...,purgeprovenance,...}/**/*.go`: *"Use repository
abstractions over interfaces so storage remains swappable"* and *"inject dependencies through
interfaces and mock at the boundary."*

## The constraint any fix must respect

The reset and the cache invalidation **must stay in one transaction.** From
`purgeprovenance.go:334-339`:

> Cache invalidation rides in the SAME transaction as the row reset because the two are one
> indivisible statement of intent: "this track's lyrics are repudiated, fetch it again." A reset
> that commits without its invalidation is precisely the data-loss defect
> (`scan.Enqueuer.EnqueuePending` consults `Cache.Lookup` BEFORE enqueueing, marks the row done
> as a cache hit, and the deleted sidecar is never rewritten), so they commit together or not at
> all.

So the seam cannot be a plain repository method that opens its own transaction. It needs to
accept a `*sql.Tx` (or be driven inside one), which is why this is a design task rather than a
mechanical extraction.

## Proposed shape

A narrow transactional interface the purger accepts, implemented by `queue`/`scan`:

```go
// Resetter re-queues rows inside a caller-supplied transaction, so the reset can
// commit atomically with whatever else the caller must commit alongside it.
type Resetter interface {
    ResetForRefetch(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx, scanResultIDs, workItemIDs []int64) (srReset, wqReset int, err error)
}
```

The purger takes a `Resetter` instead of reaching for `*sql.DB`, and the status/priority/timestamp
constants live in exactly one place — the package that owns the table.

Worth checking during design whether `ResetInstrumental` should route through the same seam. If
it should, this closes two copies rather than one; if it should not, the reason is worth writing
down.

## Acceptance

- [ ] No `status` / `priority` / `next_attempt_at` literal for `work_queue` or `scan_results`
      appears outside the package that owns the table (grep-assertable).
- [ ] The reset and cache invalidation still commit in a single transaction — a test asserts that
      a failure after the reset leaves NO partial commit.
- [ ] The purger is constructed with an interface and a test mocks it at that boundary.
- [ ] Existing `purgeprovenance` behaviour is unchanged: same rows reset, same counts returned.

## Notes

Not urgent, and deliberately not in the "Realign & Reconciliation" milestone — that milestone is
the v1.29.0 release gate, and this is a structural cleanup with no user-visible behaviour change.
Filed from the #661 review so the deferral is tracked rather than lost.

**Source:** CodeRabbit nitpick on #661, `internal/purgeprovenance/purgeprovenance.go:327-379` ("Row resets bypass the repository seam") -- https://github.com/sydlexius/canticle/pull/661#pullrequestreview-4781133997

records.title: Proposal: add DCP-style ranged compaction with context_compact_range
records.body:
Thanks for building `pi-context`. The checkpoint model is a novel way to collapse a completed phase into a clean continuation.

Would you be interested in adding **DCP-style ranged context compaction**, inspired by [OpenCode DCP](https://github.com/Opencode-DCP/opencode-dynamic-context-pruning)? I would be willing to contribute.

The proposed distinction:

- `context_compact`: branch from a checkpoint and summarize everything after it.
- `context_compact_range`: replace selected ranges in the current model-facing context while preserving later messages.

```text
A — B — [C — D] — E — F
          ↓
A — B — summary — E — F
```

## Proposed phases

### Phase 1: ranged compaction

- Add a model-callable `context_compact_range` tool.
- Accept one or more `{ start, end, summary }` ranges using stable message references.
- Persist range-compaction blocks in append-only custom session entries.
- Apply them non-destructively through Pi's `context` hook.
- Support inspection and decompression.

### Phase 2: deterministic tool-result cleanup

- Deduplicate identical tool calls.
- Prune stale failed inputs while retaining diagnostics.
- Prune reads superseded by later reads or successful writes/edits.
- Use tombstones or retrieval pointers instead of LLM summaries where possible.

Pi truncates individual tool outputs, but does not appear to age, deduplicate, or supersede them before normal prefix compaction.

### Phase 3: hierarchical compaction

- Allow ranges to include existing range-compaction blocks.
- Compact several old summaries into a higher-level summary.
- Preserve block ancestry so operations remain inspectable and reversible.

## Safety requirements

- Never rewrite the original Pi session history.
- Keep assistant tool calls and tool results atomic.
- Protect the recent working frontier by default.
- Reject invalid, stale, or overlapping ranges atomically.
- Handle native Pi compaction and tree navigation safely.
- Avoid excessive prompt-cache invalidation.

Pi's public extension API appears sufficient: `registerTool()` exposes the operation to the model, the `context` hook derives the outgoing message projection, and `appendEntry()` persists state. No Pi core changes should be required.

References:

- [Compaction in Pi](https://earendil.com/posts/compaction-in-pi/)
- [OpenCode DCP](https://github.com/Opencode-DCP/opencode-dynamic-context-pruning)

Would this fit `pi-context`, or would you prefer it as a companion extension?

This issue was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by a human before filing.

records.title: A1: layered BFS-2 + feedback APPLY (rank-only) + graph_epoch in cache key — behind density gate edges/100 ≥ 50
records.body:
Slice A1 of the Memory Graph epic #320 (ADR-0030). Size: M. Depends on #324 (A0 complete; I1–I3 standing).

## Unlock gate

`edges/100 records ≥ 50` (= edges-per-memory ≥ 0.5) — an expert threshold (1–3 auto-links per write), **revisitable at A0-review** against live minting telemetry. Explicitly a **ranking-feature MERGE unlock, NOT an access gate**. I1–I3 already stand by then (ADR-0030, Decision 3).

## Problem

A1 applies ranking mechanics once fuel density is reached — the committee's answer to "mechanics before fuel is a no-op over an empty table".

## Approach

- **App-level layered BFS-2** — `WHERE from_memory_id IN (?, ...)`; 2 levels × 2 directions = 4 point queries over indexes; a per-node fanout cap plus a total-work cap on visited rows. NOT a recursive CTE.
- **Path attribution «first anchor wins»** — a neighbour's path is its first anchor's; the ADR-0028 determinism line holds, the id tiebreak is untouched.
- **Feedback APPLY — rank-only, bounded Δ per principal** (invariant I6); never status, never eligibility (`pipeline_state` and §4 refined-only are untouchable). Effective weight = pipeline confidence × feedback factor, computed at read time; uniform-404 on the apply path.
- **Ranking formula** `(1-alpha)/(rrf_k + 2*pos) × w_edge × 0.7^(depth-1)` — a pure function of the fused ranking, the edge table, and depth; weights enter post-gate and move ranking only.
- **`graph_epoch`** — a meta counter incremented on any edge write or update, part of the CCR/assemble_context cache key — without it feedback serves stale rankings.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gate evaluation documented at A0-review (density from live telemetry); merge blocked below `edges/100 ≥ 50`.
- [ ] BFS-2 honors the fanout cap and the total-work cap; 4 indexed queries, no recursive CTE.
- [ ] APPLY is rank-only with bounded Δ per principal (tests); no path mutates status or eligibility.
- [ ] The CCR/assemble_context cache key includes `graph_epoch`; the epoch increments on edge writes/updates.
- [ ] Guard: reference recall@5 ≥ 0.9409.

Source: ADR-0030 (Decision 3; invariants I3/I6) — https://github.com/vesmaro/vesmaro/blob/main/docs/project/adr/0030-memory-graph-self-fueling.md

records.title: Leetcode #207 Course Schedule
`call_graph_url()` serializes POSIXct body fields as ambiguous, offset-less datetime strings
records.body:
`call_graph_url()` serializes JSON request bodies with:

```
# R/call_graph.R, call_graph_url()
body <- jsonlite::toJSON(body[!null], auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 22, null = "null")
```

This uses jsonlite's default POSIXt = "string" handling, which calls format()/as.character() on POSIXct values. That respects the object's tzone attribute but appends no UTC offset or "Z" suffix, so the resulting string is ambiguous about what instant it represents.

Microsoft Graph's OData Edm.DateTimeOffset fields expect an explicit ISO 8601 string with a Z or numeric offset (e.g. "2022-07-31T14:05:19Z"); sending a bare "2022-07-31 14:05:19" leaves Graph to guess the offset, which I think resolves against the site/tenant's regional timezone, silently shifting the stored instant away from the value the caller intended.

``` r
library(jsonlite)

x <- as.POSIXct(1659276319, origin = "1970-01-01", tz = "UTC")

# This mirrors call_graph_url()'s exact serialization call:
jsonlite::toJSON(
    list(dateTimeField = x),
    auto_unbox = TRUE,
    digits = 22,
    null = "null"
)
#> {"dateTimeField":"2022-07-31 14:05:19"}

# Confirming it's not just a formatting-style choice: jsonlite's "ISO8601"
# option has the same ambiguity, just with a "T" separator instead of a space
jsonlite::toJSON(list(dateTimeField = x), POSIXt = "ISO8601", auto_unbox = TRUE)
#> {"dateTimeField":"2022-07-31T14:05:19"}
#  still no "Z"/offset

# The only unambiguous encoding requires explicit UTC formatting:
strftime(x, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
#> [1] "2022-07-31T14:05:19Z"
```

<sup>Created on 2026-09-09 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

**Expected:** A POSIXct value passed in a request body to call_graph_url() should serialize to an unambiguous ISO 8601 UTC string (...Z) matching what Graph's OData Edm.DateTimeOffset fields expect, regardless of the POSIXct object's tzone attribute or the caller's Sys.timezone().

**Actual:** The serialized string carries no UTC marker at all, so any Graph endpoint accepting a dateTime/DateTimeOffset field is handed an ambiguous value whenever a caller passes a native POSIXct.

**Suggested fix:** In call_graph_url(), before calling jsonlite::toJSON(), recursively convert any POSIXct (and Date) elements of body to explicit UTC ISO 8601 strings, e.g. `strftime(x, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")` for POSIXct and `strftime(x, "%Y-%m-%d", tz = "UTC")` for Date. Neither of jsonlite's built-in POSIXt options ("string", "ISO8601") is sufficient on their own, since neither appends a UTC offset.

records.title: Create verbatim manifest formats
records.body: Each section below represents be at least one issue in this epic. Some tickets have already been created, for others we'll wait a little to see how things pan out. ## Push down HCA specifics to a `Bundle` subclass (#4940, done) The in memory representation of metadata in Azul is heavily influenced by the old DCP/1 representation of bundles in the DSS which distinguished between manifest entries and metadata. This needlessly complicates the AnVIL code and it would further complicate passing along verbatim metadata. We'll need to address this first. This boils down to removing the `.metadata_files` and `.manifest` attributes from `azul.indexer.Bundle` and leaving the definition of any metadata-related attributes up to subclasses. The requirement is that the repository and metadata plugin for any given catalog agree on the data structure referenced by these attributes. This refactoring is complicated by the fact that the current class hierarchy first differentiates by repository (TDR vs DSS) and then by atlas (AnVIL vs HCA) whereas the introduction of metadata-related repositories should occur at the atlas level. To resolve, swap the levels, use mixins or accept some degree of duplication. ~Since the AnVIL metadata plugin doesn't use the HCA Metadata API, the AnVIL repository plugin doesn't actually *need* to emulate the `links.json` structure, as it currently does. It can continue to use the adjacency list approach but should remove mentions of protocols and the HCA-specific schema cruft.~ ## Ensure that each `Bundle` instance is a complete subgraph (#4941, done) … so that it even includes entities that are not transformed into contributions, as long as the discovery of those entities isn't prohibitively expensive and their cardinality isn't prohibitively high. This is already the case for HCA since every HCA `Bundle` instance contains all entities of the respective subgraph, including the `links` entity defining the subgraph. For AnVIL this may require following more FK relations during the subgraph traversal, and adding entities currently not indexed. The goal is for an AnVIL `Bundle` instance to include all schema entities in a given subgraph, and for these entities to reflect all significant columns of the corresponding TDR table row. It does not need to cover non-schema entities. Spike to review AnVIL TDR schema, for unindexed entities, properties, or FK relations. Determine insignificant columns, if any, such as `datarepo_row_id`. Informally, an insignificant column is one that no external user of Terra would want to be present in their workspace after a hand-over. ## Represent verbatim metadata as `Document` subtype `Replica` (#4942, sub-epic, done) Each `Replica` instance will represent the significant content of a metadata entity verbatim. Unlike `Aggregate` and `Contribution`, `Replica` instances will not be segregated into separate indices by entity type. The transformers of a metadata plugin will be extended to emit `Replica` instances, in addition to the `Contribution` instances they currently emit. For most entity types, the metadata plugin will emit a replica and a contribution, for some entity types (e.g. Diagnoses) it only emits a replica. Replica documents have the following shape: ```json { "entity_type": "…", "content": {…}, "hub_ids": ["…", …] } ``` The `.entity_type` property is a string classifying replicas by type. For AnVIL replicas this is the name of the AnVIL table from which the replica originates. For HCA this is the entity type as specified in the DCP/2 spec, which happens to also be a table name. The `.content` property contains the verbatim metadata entity as supplied by the repository plugin. The `.hub_ids` property contains a list of IDs of 1) file entities the replica is derived from and 2) file entities that are derived from the replica. For now only files are used as hubs, because all of Azul's current manifest formats are generated from the aggregate index for files. In the future we may very well add more types of hub entities. A replica's hub entities aren't necessarily confined to a single bundle. When a replica document is created, its hubs all come from a single bundle but as more bundles are indexed, the replica document is updated efficiently (see below) by adding the IDs of newly discovered hubs to the `.hub_ids` property, without having to resend the potentially large value of the `.content` property. ES must be prevented from making any assumptions about replica content, from analyzing it, and from reordering array items or dictionary entries contained therein. The easiest way to do that is to map (in ES) the `.content` property of replica documents using `object` for `type` with [enabled](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/7.17/enabled.html) set to `false`. If problems arise with that approach, an alternative would be to make `content` a string containing serialized JSON, and to map it as `text` with `enabled` and `doc_values` set to `false`. Replica documents are content-addressed: a document's ID is the hash of the value of its `.content` property. This enables us to optimistically create replicas with `PUT //_create/<_id>` (or to `PUT //_doc/<_id>` with `"op_type": "create"`). If that request fails with 409, we know that 1) the replica already exists and 2) that its `.content` is up-to-date. We can then follow up with a `POST //_update/<_id>` to update just the `.hub_ids` property (see below) using a [scripted update](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/7.17/docs-update.html). [Edit @nadove-ucsc] TODO: What happens with stale replicas (same entity ID, but different content hash, due to outdated contents)? This scenario should only occur when we do incremental indexing, so we can probably ignore this for now. https://github.com/Da
